title: Liwiro Platform Foundations
summary: The system map for Liwiro, Verun, Verse, VI, generated services, and the data/runtime boundaries between them.
audience: Verse agents, platform operators, service authors
agentGoals: Identify which surface owns a task before proposing a command or route.
Understand how Liwiro, Verse, VI, generated services, and VDB interact.
Avoid mixing control-plane actions with runtime-service actions.
prerequisites: Liwiro frontend and backend are running.
VDB transport is configured and reachable.
The agent knows whether the task is UI, CLI, service-runtime, or VDB-native.
requiredWorkflows: Start in Liwiro when the task is setup, service generation, service operations, VDB portal work, VI portal work, or Verse chat.
Use the Service Builder to define LAPIS contracts, then the Service Manager to operate generated services.
Use VDB Console for direct VQL/VDB operations and Versa Console for Versa source files and REPL work.
guardrails: Do not treat Liwiro frontend auth as the same thing as VDB authentication.
Do not assume generated services can use VDB until VDB credentials are configured and authenticated.
Do not invent routes or subsystems that do not exist in the platform.
antiPatterns: Sending a user to VDB Console for tasks that belong in Service Builder or Service Manager.
Treating Verse Chat advice as if it already changed runtime state.
Confusing VI files with service-inline Versa scripts.
examples_good: A task to create a new microservice starts with a LAPIS config in Service Builder, not with raw VQL in VDB Console.
A task to inspect existing data uses VDB Console or a generated service endpoint after VDB auth is confirmed.
A task to debug script syntax uses Versa validation and VI/Versa runtime guidance before proposing fixes.
examples_bad: Telling an agent to patch VDB data directly when the user asked for a service contract change.
Using generated-service runtime docs to answer a Liwiro setup question.
Assuming a Verse AI action card already executed a backend change.
failure_modes: Wrong-surface recommendations cause broken instructions and skipped prerequisites.
Auth-layer confusion causes agents to call VDB or protected services without valid credentials.
Missing system boundaries leads to incorrect LAPIS, Versa, or VQL advice.

title: Authentication and Access Boundaries
summary: The required distinctions between Liwiro platform auth, service bearer auth, and VDB runtime authentication.
audience: Verse agents, platform admins, generated-service authors
agentGoals: Separate platform login, service auth, and VDB auth every time.
Know which auth prerequisite must be satisfied before each action.
Avoid unsafe assumptions about inherited or shared sessions.
prerequisites: The Liwiro platform may have a frontend session.
Generated services may require bearer tokens that are unrelated to the frontend session.
VDB operations require successful VDB authentication and active domain/database context.
requiredWorkflows: Authenticate to VDB before running VDB queries, creating collections, switching domains, or executing VDB-backed Versa code.
Use bearer auth only for generated-service endpoints that explicitly require it.
Treat setup/bootstrap credentials as control-plane inputs, not as general runtime credentials.
guardrails: Never use VDB without authenticating it first.
Never assume a Liwiro login gives direct VDB data access.
Never describe a protected service endpoint as public unless LAPIS says `requiresAuth: false`.
antiPatterns: Calling VDB immediately after startup without verifying credentials or workspace context.
Reusing bearer tokens as if they are VDB credentials.
Treating auth service setup keys as long-term operator credentials.
examples_good: Before a VDB read, verify auth succeeded and the correct domain/database context has been selected.
Before invoking a protected endpoint, provide an Authorization bearer token and describe its purpose.
When an auth-dependent service proxies signin, distinguish upstream auth-service behavior from local service behavior.
examples_bad: Trying to use VDB in Versa without `vdb.auth(...)` and `vdb.set(...)` succeeding first.
Answering a VDB RBAC question with only frontend login guidance.
Claiming an endpoint is reachable because the platform UI is open.
failure_modes: VDB auth failures surface as runtime errors before data access or script execution can proceed.
Bearer-protected endpoints return 401 when tokens are absent or invalid.
Auth confusion leads to incorrect troubleshooting and invalid generated code.

title: LAPIS and Generated Service Lifecycle
summary: How LAPIS contracts are normalized, validated, generated, operated, and repaired inside Liwiro.
agentGoals: Produce valid LAPIS payloads for Service Builder.
Understand how metadata, auth, models, modules, and endpoints affect runtime generation.
Use validation output to repair configs instead of guessing.
prerequisites: A LAPIS config must normalize into metadata, auth, models, sharedModules, modules, and endpoints.
Every generated service has a VDB domain/workspace expectation and a runtime env shape.
Validation happens before generation and should be treated as authoritative.
requiredWorkflows: Normalize the LAPIS contract first, then validate it, then generate the service runtime.
For CRUD endpoints, require `crudOperation` and `linkedModel`.
For custom endpoints, require a readable VDB command string in `vqlQuery`.
For script endpoints, require non-empty `versaScript` and valid runtime assumptions.
guardrails: Do not propose endpoint shapes that conflict with LAPIS validation rules.
Do not skip model existence checks for `linkedModel`.
Do not mark a service as valid until dry-run validation succeeds.
antiPatterns: Using free-form text where a readable VDB command is required.
Creating script endpoints with no Versa script body.
Treating Service Builder validation as optional before generation.
examples_good: A CRUD read endpoint declares `operationType: crud`, `crudOperation: read`, and a real `linkedModel`.
A custom VQL endpoint stores a readable VDB command string, in `vqlQuery`.
A service with script endpoints is repaired based on returned validation errors until dry-run passes.
examples_bad: A custom endpoint whose `vqlQuery` is a JSON command object instead of readable command text.
A linked model reference to a model that does not exist in `models`.
Assuming generation is correct because schema validation passed once.
failure_modes: Schema and semantic errors block generation immediately.
Versa parse/runtime issues block script endpoints.
Dry-run execution failures expose hidden startup, auth, and side-effect problems.

title: LAPIS Reference
summary: The contract rules for metadata, auth, models, modules, and endpoint definitions used by Liwiro generation.
audience: Verse agents writing or repairing LAPIS
agentGoals: Emit valid LAPIS structures without inventing unsupported keys or endpoint modes.
Choose the correct endpoint type: CRUD, custom VQL, or script.
Respect docs and auth configuration inside metadata/auth.
prerequisites: The top-level contract is a JSON object.
`metadata.apiName`, `metadata.basePath`, and semantic `metadata.version` are required.
Endpoint methods and paths must be explicit.
requiredWorkflows: Use `crud` for generated collection-backed behavior.
Use `custom` only when you need a portal-style flat action VQL object.
Use `script` only when CRUD/custom cannot express the behavior and the Versa runtime assumptions are known.
guardrails: Keep `basePath` rooted with `/`.
Keep `version` semantic, such as `1.0.0`.
Do not mix VQL text syntax into `vqlQuery`; it must decode to a flat action object.
antiPatterns: Inventing unsupported `operationType` values.
Using untyped or incomplete field definitions.
Assuming route auth rules are implied rather than declared.
examples_good: A metadata block with `apiName`, `basePath`, `version`, `database`, and optional `documentation` config.
A model whose fields specify name, type, and required state.
An auth service definition that clearly separates auth model, endpoints, and password-reset behavior.
examples_bad: A route with `operationType: versa` instead of the supported `script` alias expected after normalization.
A model field missing its name or type.
A version string like `v1` instead of semantic versioning.
failure_modes: Normalization may coerce aliases, but invalid contracts still fail validation.
Bad endpoint semantics stop the service before runtime generation.
Weak docs/auth configuration produces confusing or inaccessible runtime behavior.

title: Versa Runtime Reference
summary: Agent-facing guidance for writing flawless Versa code in Liwiro and VI, including imports, runtime objects, and VDB prerequisites.
audience: Verse agents generating Versa or fixing script endpoints
agentGoals: Write valid Versa syntax that matches the VI parser/runtime.
Import required modules before use and keep imports at the top.
Handle runtime objects such as `params`, `service`, `auth`, and VDB setup correctly.
prerequisites: Versa imports must be declared before executable code.
Generated script routes receive runtime objects such as `params`, `service`, and `auth`.
VDB access in Versa requires `vdb.auth(...)` to succeed before `vdb.set(...)` and any data operation.
requiredWorkflows: Declare required imports first, then compute inputs, then perform guarded operations.
Authenticate VDB and set context before any VDB reads or writes.
When fixing parser/runtime errors, use the returned error plus the offending construct to repair the script.
guardrails: Do not use a module namespace without importing it.
Do not use VDB before authenticating it first.
Do not assume async/await, decorators, enums, or TypeScript-like constructs exist unless documented.
antiPatterns: Using `vdb.read(...)` or `vdb.create(...)` before `vdb.auth(...)` and `vdb.set(...)`.
Placing imports after executable code.
Treating `params` runtime objects as if they are globally defined outside the script environment.
examples_good: A script imports `json_xml`, `vdb`, and other required modules before defining logic.
A route validates input from `params`, authenticates VDB, sets context, and only then performs data operations.
A repair flow changes the specific undefined module or parser error rather than rewriting unrelated code.
examples_bad: Calling VDB immediately with no authentication handshake.
Using `http` or `email` namespaces without imports.
Returning malformed objects because the script never normalizes input.
failure_modes: Missing imports trigger runtime namespace errors.
Bad syntax or unsupported constructs fail parser validation.
VDB auth/context errors fail script execution before business logic runs.

title: Versa Console and Versa Execution Runtime
summary: How VI files, REPL work, and service-inline Versa execution differ, and what runtime assumptions agents must preserve.
audience: Verse agents and operators working in VI or script-backed services
agentGoals: Know when code runs as a VI file versus as a generated service script.
Understand the local source workspace and validation path.
Avoid assuming file-based behavior inside inline service scripts.
prerequisites: Versa Console works with local `.versa` source files and a terminal/REPL surface.
Generated service scripts are wrapped with runtime params and VDB context setup.
Parser validation and runtime execution are related but not identical.
requiredWorkflows: Use Versa Console for source-file authoring and iterative syntax repair.
Use service validation for inline LAPIS `versaScript` behavior.
Treat REPL/file tasks and inline route tasks as different runtime surfaces.
guardrails: Do not assume a VI file has the same runtime params as a service-inline script.
Do not mix portal file paths with inline script hints carelessly.
Do not skip validation just because a script ran in a different context once.
antiPatterns: Copying a file-oriented Versa example into an inline route without adapting params and service context.
Treating temporary validation paths as persisted user files.
Using VI runtime success as proof that service startup will succeed.
examples_good: Use Versa Console for exploratory coding, then adapt the logic to route-scoped runtime params for LAPIS scripts.
Treat validation file paths as hints, not production paths.
Use parser feedback to fix imports and unsupported constructs before runtime testing.
examples_bad: Assuming `params.service` exists in every standalone file.
Writing service docs that tell users to run inline route code directly from the filesystem.
Ignoring different VDB context rules between standalone and generated runtime execution.
failure_modes: Context mismatch causes scripts to pass parse validation but fail at runtime.
Wrong file/runtime assumptions produce confusing repair loops.
Agents recommend commands that belong to the wrong execution surface.

title: VDB Runtime Reference
summary: The operational model for VDB authentication, sessions, domains, databases, collections, scripts, exports, RBAC, and TUMI.
audience: Verse agents writing VDB or guiding portal operations
agentGoals: Form correct VDB workflows with explicit auth and workspace context.
Understand the difference between reads, writes, admin actions, scripts, and exports.
Recognize when a VDB action is risky or permission-sensitive.
prerequisites: VDB requires valid credentials and an active session.
Domain and database context matter before most collection operations.
Administrative actions may need higher privileges than ordinary reads.
requiredWorkflows: Authenticate first, then select domain, then select database, then operate on collections or scripts.
Use reads for inspection and writes/admin actions only when the request explicitly requires them.
Treat exports, TUMI actions, and RBAC changes as high-risk operations.
guardrails: Never use VDB without authenticating it first.
Never describe administrative actions as harmless reads.
Never skip domain/database context selection when a query depends on workspace scope.
antiPatterns: Querying collections before a domain/database is selected.
Treating scripts, exports, and TUMI operations as ordinary data reads.
Assuming super-admin capabilities in examples that should work for ordinary users.
examples_good: Auth succeeds, context is set, and only then a collection read is attempted.
A high-risk export is described with permission checks and operator confirmation.
RBAC/TUMI guidance is separated from normal document CRUD guidance.
examples_bad: Jumping straight to a `create` or `delete` command with no session or context.
Using VDB script creation in examples that are supposed to be dry-run safe.
Writing examples that hide the target domain/database.
failure_modes: Authentication failures block all downstream operations.
Wrong workspace context produces missing-collection or wrong-data behavior.
Admin actions without proper permissions fail and may be unsafe to retry blindly.

title: VQL Reference
summary: The readable command syntax and query semantics used by VDB Console, custom LAPIS endpoints, and VDB-backed runtime work.
agentGoals: Produce portal-ready and LAPIS-ready readable VDB commands.
Distinguish read, create, update, delete, define, use, list, script, export, index, and domain lifecycle actions.
Avoid JSON command envelopes.
prerequisites: VQL payloads used by Liwiro custom endpoints must decode to readable VDB command strings.
Collection-level operations depend on VDB auth and active workspace context.
Args, query, and data sections should be explicit when needed.
Domain lifecycle actions use `domain_status`, `domain_suspend`, or `domain_resume` with an explicit `domain` field.
requiredWorkflows: Represent VQL as a readable command string, when used in Liwiro.
Keep query filters and data updates in the correct sections.
Use the smallest safe action family that matches the task.
guardrails: Do not place raw command strings into `vqlQuery`.
Do not mix unrelated action families in one payload unless the runtime explicitly supports it.
Do not describe destructive commands as examples without a warning.
Treat suspend and resume as ownership-controlled domain operations; do not omit the domain or imply they are collection commands.
antiPatterns: Using a shell-like VQL string where JSON is required.
Putting update data in a find query.
Leaving the target collection/domain ambiguous.
examples_good: A read payload uses `action: find`, `collection`, `where`, and optional `limit` fields.
An update payload uses `action: update`, `collection`, `where`, and `set` fields.
A custom LAPIS endpoint stores a parsed flat action object in `vqlQuery`.
A domain status check uses `{action: domain_status, domain: "example"}`; suspend/resume use the same flat shape with the corresponding action.
examples_bad: A custom endpoint with `vqlQuery: "read users where ..."`.
A create payload that omits the target collection.
A destructive command presented without caution or auth assumptions.
failure_modes: Malformed objects fail validation or VDB execution.
Wrong query/data placement causes incorrect runtime semantics.
Ambiguous workspace assumptions break otherwise valid payloads.

title: Verse Agents and Retrieval Reference
summary: How Verse routes work, how capability/manual context is selected, and how agents should ground answers in the shared corpus.
audience: Verse agent maintainers and advanced operators
agentGoals: Route work to the right subsystem guidance before answering.
Prefer shared-corpus facts over invented behavior.
Keep capability recommendations aligned with real platform surfaces.
prerequisites: Verse may combine persona, skills, capability metadata, and docs retrieval.
Manual links in platform capabilities should resolve to shared-corpus wiki pages.
Agent responses should expose blockers and prerequisites explicitly.
requiredWorkflows: When a query mentions LAPIS, VDB, Versa, VQL, or Liwiro operations, retrieve the matching subsystem docs first.
When a request is risky, mention the guardrail before giving a runnable action.
When documentation is missing or conflicting, say so instead of inventing unsupported behavior.
guardrails: Do not use removed canonical-doc routes or outdated corpus fragments.
Do not claim support for constructs the shared corpus marks as undocumented or unsafe.
Do not skip auth or dry-run prerequisites in generated guidance.
antiPatterns: Mixing old `verse-verun-reference` assumptions with new shared-corpus guidance.
Returning VDB guidance without the authentication prerequisite.
Answering Versa repair questions without grounding in runtime rules.
examples_good: A Verse agent answering a VDB question cites auth, workspace selection, and VQL shape in order.
A Verse agent answering a LAPIS question grounds the answer in endpoint semantics and validation behavior.
A Verse agent states when a requested construct is undocumented rather than fabricating syntax.
examples_bad: Linking to removed canonical wiki views.
Providing a confident answer from stale docs fragments.
Skipping retrieval and relying on unsupported memory for critical runtime rules.
failure_modes: Stale docs references lead to wrong or broken agent guidance.
Missing prerequisites produce unsafe recommendations.
Capability links drift if they are not kept aligned with shared-corpus slugs.

title: Dry-Run Validation Contract
summary: The required behavior of Liwiro validation when it performs real runtime execution with strict live VDB auth and side-effect suppression.
audience: Verse agents, service authors, and backend maintainers
agentGoals: Understand what validation proves and what it blocks.
Use returned dry-run errors to repair LAPIS, Versa, and runtime assumptions.
Explain why a service is invalid when startup, auth, or endpoint execution fails.
prerequisites: Dry-run validation still authenticates against live VDB.
Dry-run validation executes the generated runtime in memory or test mode rather than writing deployable artifacts.
Side effects must be suppressed even though the code path is real.
requiredWorkflows: Run schema/normalization validation first, then Versa static validation, then dry-run runtime execution.
Fail validation if live VDB authentication or context setup cannot be established.
Suppress filesystem writes, outbound HTTP, email sending, and VDB mutations while preserving actionable error reporting.
guardrails: Dry-run is not a mock-only success path; it must fail on real auth/setup problems.
Reads may occur only after auth succeeds and only when they do not mutate state.
Validation output must identify which endpoint or startup phase failed.
antiPatterns: Marking a service valid after only schema checks.
Allowing validation to write indexes, documents, scripts, files, or external requests.
Hiding auth/setup failures behind generic success or warning messages.
examples_good: Validation reports that VDB auth failed before any route dry-run could execute.
Validation blocks an outbound HTTP call and returns a dry-run suppression error tied to the endpoint.
Validation executes a safe script path, returns structured results, and flags skipped writes explicitly.
examples_bad: Validation passes because the app object was created even though VDB auth was broken.
Dry-run sends real email or writes real data.
Returned errors do not identify the failing route or startup step.
failure_modes: Live VDB auth failure invalidates the service immediately.
Suppressed side effects surface as dry-run execution errors or notices.
Endpoint-specific runtime errors drive the repair loop for LAPIS and Versa.
